Lessons.Title: Use Properties to Multiply Decimals
ExplanationParagraphs: Original IM2021 Grade5 Unit5 Lesson19 applies associative/distributive/compensation strategies and asks learners to SORT an actual publisher card deck in TWO different ways, first by their chosen mathematical category, then match expressions to cards A,B,C. The printed full card deck is NOT decoded from teacher HTML: no invented card values are certified as source.
Warm-up original four number talks40×2×0.1=8,20×0.1×4=8,0.1×80=8 and0.01×20×40=8. Explain why associativity and place-value scaling yield equal results.

Activity1 original Decimal Multiplication Card Sort has source image/card deck not independently readable; teachers distribute original physical cards. Children justify two ways to sort and add a new expression equivalent to each A,B,C. Previous independent card A6×0.24, B5×3.8, C7×0.35 are clearly labeled Edulytiks extra examples rather than unrecovered printed card values.

Activity2 original source numeric products6×0.12=0.72,4×1.4=5.6,5×3.9=19.5 and25×0.41=10.25. Encourage choice between decimal-unit whole products, distribution and nearby whole compensation, explaining each.

Optional Activity3 original source35×0.08=2.8,35×0.7=24.5,35×0.78=27.3 and42×0.66=27.72. Source card sort, original figure rights and learner justifications remain TEACHER_REVIEW_REQUIRED; independently authored cooldown is separate from publisher gated source.

Source and assessment limits: independently authored Edulytiks Cool-down with teacher-reviewed drawing/explanation. Original publisher gated Cool-down, standalone student PDF and original image binaries are not individually certified. Numeric exact choices cover only eligible subskills, not the original open source tasks.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Goal: sort different multiplication expressions by shared mathematical structure and by equal numerical value, then justify matches using associative, distributive and compensation properties. The original 2021 task first lets learners invent categories for an expression-card sort, then asks for matched equivalent expressions and a new equivalent expression, so it is not a single product quiz.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Warm-up: mentally decide whether 6×0.24 is closer to one or two whole units; compare this magnitude with 6×24=144 hundredths and explain why 1.44 is plausible. The estimate is a reasonableness check, not a proof of a particular sorting category.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 1 — original equivalence card groups: card A is 6×0.24. Match A to 6×(0.2+0.04), (6×24)×0.01 and 6×0.2+6×0.04, which all yield 1.44. Card B is 5×3.8. Match it to 5×(4−0.2) and 20−1, both 19. Card C is 7×0.35, matching (7×35)×0.01 and 7×0.3+7×0.05, both 2.45. Ask learners to invent TWO different ways of grouping the expression cards, by use of compensation versus distributive versus whole-number scaling, and by equivalent value.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 2 — select a strategy: find 24×0.61 by using 24×61 hundredths=14.64 or 24×(0.6+0.01)=14.4+0.24=14.64. Compare with 8×2.9=8×3−8×0.1=23.2. Write one new matching expression for one of the examples and justify the preservation of quantities rather than only the resulting number.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Assessment: the source asks students to justify choices of categories, matches, a novel equivalent expression, and why a strategy works; an isolated numeric equality is a subcheck, not evidence that card sorting and explanation occurred. Source card image set and secured Cool-down are not reused.

KeyConcepts.Title: Distributive decimal product
KeyConcepts.Definition: Break one decimal factor into a sum of tenths and hundredths, multiply both parts and add.

KeyConcepts.Title: Associate to a whole-number product
KeyConcepts.Definition: Factor hundredth or tenth units out and use familiar integer multiplication.

KeyConcepts.Title: Compensation near a whole
KeyConcepts.Definition: Subtract the difference from a nearby whole number after multiplying that whole.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Match cards solely because they share printed digits
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Equivalent expressions can have different mathematical structure, and same digits can represent different values.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Interpret which decimal units and properties create equivalence before matching.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Subtract only the correction fraction without multiplying it by the whole-number factor
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The distributive property applies to every term.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Invent source A/B/C card deck content from a first-party example whose publisher card image is inaccessible
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The original IM2021 printed student activities use specific decimal values and require place-value reasoning, so substituting unrelated examples or accepting a right-justified digit alignment does not preserve source parity.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Restore printed warmup and all eight actual task products; keep source card matching teacher-only with explicit uncertainty.

SummaryPoints: Original source card deck not fabricated and teacher reviewed.
Optional prior: The same product can have whole-fact, distributive or compensation representations.
Optional prior: Inventing and justifying multiple sorting categories remains teacher-reviewed.
Optional prior: A learner-created valid new expression is evidence beyond a memorized decimal product.

Lessons.Title: Products in the Hundredths Place PLC Activity
ExplanationParagraphs: Original IM2021 Grade5 U05:L20 Products in the Hundredths Place introduces why multiplying TWO quantities of TENTHS yields HUNDREDTHS of the original one whole; a 10×10 area grid and fractional units are essential conceptual representations.
Warm-up source asks explicitly 1×0.1=0.1 and0.1×0.1=0.01, not a different4×0.3 warmup. Learners explain that one tenth of one tenth is one hundredth of the SAME unit.

Activity1 original2×0.3=0.6 versus0.2×0.3=0.06. Kiran incorrectly writes0.2×0.4=0.8; correct0.08. Teacher asks why product of two factors less than one is smaller than either in this positive unit interval, with original source grid drawing.
Activity2 original1.8×0.4=0.72,2.5×0.6=1.50,3.8×0.7=2.66. Related comparisons74×6=444,7.4×6=44.4 and7.4×0.6=4.44 demonstrate how unit scaling affects the product by powers of10.

Preserve correct but invented0.3×0.6 and3.6×0.7 examples as optional Edulytiks extensions only. Original grids, Kiran's written argument and original gated Cool-down are not claimed fully recovered; independent Edulytiks cooldown teacher assesses grid and reasoning.

Source and assessment limits: independently authored Edulytiks Cool-down with teacher-reviewed drawing/explanation. Original publisher gated Cool-down, standalone student PDF and original image binaries are not individually certified. Numeric exact choices cover only eligible subskills, not the original open source tasks.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Goal: show why a tenth TIMES a tenth produces hundredths of the original unit, using equal-area 10×10 grids, fraction meaning, and integer products. The source explicitly contrasts 2×0.3 with0.2×0.3, then critiques an answer that is ten times too large; it extends to mixed whole-and-tenths factors and compares related products.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Warm-up: first compare 4×0.3=1.2 with 0.4×0.3=0.12. Explain why four groups of three tenths are not the same as four tenths of three tenths. The decimal point is a size statement about the factors, not a formatting rule.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 1 — two decimal factors: use a first-party unit square split into ten equal columns and ten equal rows. The intersection of three selected columns and six selected rows contains18 of100 equal cells, so 0.3×0.6=0.18 square unit. Reject the claim that the product is1.8 because one factor is less than one and the intersection covers fewer than a full unit.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 2 — whole plus fractional tenths: calculate 2.4×0.5 as24 tenths×5 tenths =120 hundredths =1.20. Compare with 2.4×5=12.0, ten times greater. Calculate 3.6×0.7 as36×7 hundredths=252 hundredths=2.52 and explain why the result can be greater than one even though one factor is less than one; the other factor is greater than one.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Assessment: source requires drawn area cells, explanations of the two factor meanings, and exact relationships between whole and decimal products, including student critique. A correct decimal multiplication answer alone cannot verify that a shaded grid depicts the two fractional side lengths.

KeyConcepts.Title: Tenths times tenths
KeyConcepts.Definition: Each tenth of one linear unit times a tenth of the perpendicular linear unit gives one hundredth of unit square.

KeyConcepts.Title: Multiply integer counts of fractional units
KeyConcepts.Definition: Two decimal tenths factors can be reexpressed as integers multiplied by a one-hundredth area unit.

KeyConcepts.Title: Related whole products change scale
KeyConcepts.Definition: Multiplying the same decimal factor by five instead of half multiplies the result by ten.
KeyConcepts.Example: Factor size explains which product is larger.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: That answer counts tenths where the area grid creates hundredths, and exceeds one factor despite both below one.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Count hundredth cells in a 10×10 whole square.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assume a product must always be smaller than both inputs
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A multiplier between0 and1 decreases the other positive factor, but if the OTHER factor exceeds one the product may still exceed one.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Check 3.6×0.7=2.52: it is less than3.6 but greater than0.7.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Claim Kiran's 0.2×0.4=0.8 is correct, or use fictional grid product0.3×0.6 as printed source
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The original IM2021 printed student activities use specific decimal values and require place-value reasoning, so substituting unrelated examples or accepting a right-justified digit alignment does not preserve source parity.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Restore the original factor pairs and exact scaled products; review original 100-square intersection visually.

SummaryPoints: Optional prior: A tenth of a tenth produces a hundredth-sized area, not another tenth.
Optional prior: Related integer products justify the hundredths scale.
Optional prior: Drawing and critiquing the fraction-area representation remain teacher-reviewed.
